title: Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion
scopeHtml: Scope: LSP contracts and violations, ISP, DIP, dependency injection and testing with fakes and mocks, and how the five principles combine.

notes.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
notes.html:
If code works with a base type, it must keep working when you pass any subtype. A subclass must honour the promises (contract) of its parent: it may do more, never less, and must not surprise callers.

The contract rules: a subtype may weaken preconditions (accept more), strengthen postconditions (promise more), must keep invariants, and must not throw new unexpected exception types.

// Classic violation
class Rectangle { int w, h; void setW(int x){w=x;} void setH(int x){h=x;} int area(){return w*h;} }
class Square extends Rectangle {
    @Override void setW(int x){ w=x; h=x; }   // surprise side effect
    @Override void setH(int x){ w=x; h=x; }
}
// caller: r.setW(5); r.setH(4); expects 20, Square gives 16
// Fix: do not inherit just because "is-a" in maths; model by behaviour
interface Shape { fun area(): Int }
data class Rect(val w: Int, val h: Int) : Shape { override fun area() = w * h }
data class Sq(val s: Int) : Shape { override fun area() = s * s }

Worked example. Bird.fly() with Penguin extends Bird throwing UnsupportedOperationException. A list of 1,000 birds in a loop crashes on the first penguin. Fix: split Bird and FlyingBird, so a penguin never promises flight.

Industry examples. java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList returns a List that throws on add: a known LSP wart in the JDK. Android ListAdapter subclasses must keep the getItemCount contract. Kotlin immutable List vs MutableList is exactly this fix.

Decision gravity. Prefer composition when "is-a" is shaky. Fixing a violating hierarchy after clients depend on it is a breaking change (one-way door).

Everyday analogy. A rental car company promises "a car". If one rental has no brakes, customers cannot use the fleet without checking each car first.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering only with Square/Rectangle. Give a second, real one (read-only collection, Penguin).
  • Saying LSP is about syntax; it is about behaviour.
  • Overriding a method to do nothing or throw, then calling it "just a special case".

notes.title: Interface Segregation Principle
notes.html:
Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one fat one.

A fat interface causes: empty or throwing implementations, recompiles when unrelated methods change, and heavy mocks in tests.

// BEFORE: fat
interface Worker { void work(); void eat(); void sleep(); }
class Robot implements Worker { public void work(){} public void eat(){ throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } public void sleep(){ throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } }

// AFTER: segregated
interface Workable { void work(); }
interface Feedable { void eat(); }
class Human implements Workable, Feedable { public void work(){} public void eat(){} }
class Robot2 implements Workable { public void work(){} }
interface Workable { fun work() }
interface Feedable { fun eat() }
class Robot : Workable { override fun work() {} }
Fat:  Client A --\             Slim:  Client A --> [Reader]
      Client B ----> [Repo 12 methods]     Client B --> [Writer]
      Client C --/                          Client C --> [Reader][Writer]

Worked example. UserRepository with 14 methods; a screen only reads names. Its test mocks 14 methods (about 25 lines). With a UserReader interface of 2 methods, the mock is 3 lines and the screen cannot accidentally delete users.

Industry examples. Java Runnable, Supplier, Comparable are one-method interfaces. Android click listeners are separate (OnClickListener, OnLongClickListener) instead of one giant Listener. Room DAOs, Kotlin Flow readers vs MutableStateFlow writers (StateFlow exposes read-only).

Decision gravity. Splitting an interface later is mostly additive (reversible: the old fat interface can extend the small ones). Merging after callers depend on pieces is harder.

Everyday analogy. A remote with 80 buttons when you only press 4. Separate small remotes for TV and AC are simpler to use and replace.

Common interview traps.

  • Making one interface per method everywhere; split by client need, not mechanically.
  • Confusing ISP with SRP: SRP is about a class's reasons to change, ISP about what a client sees.

notes.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
notes.html:
High-level policy should not depend on low-level detail; both depend on an abstraction. Also: abstractions should not depend on details.

"Inversion" means the arrow flips. Instead of OrderService -> MySqlDatabase, you write OrderService -> OrderRepository (interface) <- MySqlOrderRepository. The interface is owned by the high-level side.

// BEFORE: hard-wired
class OrderService { private final MySqlRepo repo = new MySqlRepo(); }

// AFTER
interface OrderRepository { void save(Order o); Order find(long id); }
class MySqlRepo implements OrderRepository { /* JDBC */ public void save(Order o){} public Order find(long id){ return null; } }
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    OrderService(OrderRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }   // injected
}
class OrderService(private val repo: OrderRepository)

Worked example. Swapping MySQL for Postgres: change one binding, 0 lines in OrderService. A hard-wired design needs edits in every service that calls new MySqlRepo(): about 30 files in a mid-size app.

Industry examples. Clean Architecture and hexagonal "ports and adapters" are DIP at scale. Android: Repository interface in domain, Room/Retrofit implementations in data. Spring's @Autowired, Dagger/Hilt, Koin all supply implementations.

Decision gravity. Put the interface where the consumer lives. Adding it early is cheap and reversible; but an interface with a single implementation and no test need is just noise.

Everyday analogy. A lamp and a wall socket: the lamp depends on the socket standard, not on a particular power plant.

Common interview traps.

  • DIP is not Dependency Injection. DIP is the design rule; DI is one way to supply the object.
  • Interface for every class "because DIP". Only at boundaries that vary or need faking.
  • Putting the interface in the low-level module (then the arrow does not invert).

notes.title: DI and testing
notes.html:
Dependency Injection means a class receives its collaborators instead of creating them. Three flavours: constructor (preferred), setter, field/method. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and objects immutable.

class FakeRepo implements OrderRepository {
    Map<Long, Order> m = new HashMap<>();
    public void save(Order o){ m.put(o.id, o); }
    public Order find(long id){ return m.get(id); }
}
// test: no DB, runs in ~1 ms
OrderService s = new OrderService(new FakeRepo());
class FakeRepo : OrderRepository {
    val m = mutableMapOf<Long, Order>()
    override fun save(o: Order) { m[o.id] = o }
    override fun find(id: Long) = m[id]
}
@Test fun saves() { val s = OrderService(FakeRepo()); /* act, assert */ }

Worked example. 500 service tests: with a real DB at 80 ms each = 40 s per run; with fakes at 1 ms = 0.5 s. That difference decides whether developers run tests on every save.

Fake vs mock vs stub. Stub returns canned data; fake is a working light implementation (in-memory map); mock verifies calls (Mockito verify). Prefer fakes for state, mocks sparingly for interactions like "email sent once".

Industry examples. Hilt @Module + @Binds, Spring @Configuration, Koin module { single<OrderRepository> { MySqlRepo() } }. Compile-time DI (Dagger) catches missing bindings at build time; reflection DI (Spring) at startup.

Decision gravity. Wire everything in ONE composition root. Service-locator style (calling a global get()) hides dependencies and is hard to undo.

Everyday analogy. A chef is given ingredients instead of walking out to farm them; at test time you hand in fake ingredients.

Common interview traps.

  • Using new inside business classes, then saying "I will mock it" (needs PowerMock hacks).
  • Injecting the whole DI container (service locator anti-pattern).
  • Too many constructor params (7+) is an SRP smell, not a DI problem.

notes.title: How the five fit together
notes.html:
S  small focused classes   -> easy to test and swap
O  extend by adding code   -> no regression in old code
L  subtypes keep promises  -> polymorphism is safe
I  slim interfaces         -> light mocks, fewer breaks
D  depend on abstractions  -> plug in implementations / fakes

Worked example (mini design). Notification system: Notifier interface (D, I), EmailNotifier, PushNotifier (O, L: both honour send contract without extra exceptions), OrderService only builds the message (S) and receives List<Notifier> by constructor. Adding SMS = one class + one binding.

Trade-offs in an interview. Say: "I start simple, introduce the interface when a second implementation or a test seam appears." That sentence shows judgement.

Common interview traps.

  • Listing principles without a single code example.
  • Not admitting costs: more files, more indirection, harder navigation.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• LSP: subtypes must honour the parent contract; if you override to throw or surprise, redesign (composition or split types).
  • ISP: many small client-focused interfaces; a fat interface forces dummy methods and heavy mocks.
  • DIP: policy depends on an abstraction it owns; details implement it.
  • DI is the technique (constructor injection preferred); one composition root; fakes make tests fast.
  • DIP is not DI; SRP is not ISP; do not add an interface without a second implementation or test need.
  • Name costs: extra files and indirection. Apply at boundaries, not everywhere.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle? Give an example other than Square and Rectangle.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Square/Rectangle is memorised; a second real example shows you understand behavioural contracts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If code works with a base type, it must keep working with any subtype. A subclass may accept more and promise more, but must not accept less, promise less, break invariants or throw surprising exceptions. Example: Penguin extends Bird with fly() throwing; a loop over 1,000 birds crashes on the first penguin.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LSP is about behaviour, not syntax: the code compiles but callers get surprised. Rules: weaken preconditions (accept more), strengthen postconditions (promise more), keep invariants, no new unexpected exceptions. Fix by modelling behaviour: Bird and FlyingBird, so a penguin never promises flight. JDK wart: Collections.unmodifiableList returns a List whose add throws. Kotlin's List vs MutableList is exactly the fix.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Bird { void eat(); }
interface FlyingBird extends Bird { void fly(); }
class Sparrow implements FlyingBird { public void eat() {} public void fly() {} }
class Penguin implements Bird { public void eat() {} }
interface Bird { fun eat() }
interface FlyingBird : Bird { fun fly() }
class Penguin : Bird { override fun eat() {} }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Answering only with Square/Rectangle.
  • Saying LSP is about syntax.
  • Overriding to do nothing or throw and calling it a "special case".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which rule does an override that throws break? -> Postcondition and exceptions contract.
  2. Can a subclass accept a wider input? -> Yes, weakening preconditions is allowed.
  3. Fixing a violating hierarchy after release? -> Breaking change (one-way door); prefer composition early.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the shape example. Senior speaks in contracts, gives a JDK example and prefers composition when "is-a" is shaky.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A read-only cache subclass of a mutable Store threw on put, crashing a batch job that treated all stores alike.

questions.promptHtml: What does the Interface Segregation Principle say, and how is it different from SRP?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They want the client perspective and to see you do not blur ISP with SRP.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use, so I prefer several small interfaces over one fat one. SRP is about a class's reasons to change; ISP is about what a client sees. A fat interface causes empty or throwing implementations, needless recompiles and heavy mocks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Worker{work, eat, sleep} forces Robot to throw on eat. Split into Workable and Feedable. A UserRepository with 14 methods needs a 25-line mock for a screen that reads names; a 2-method UserReader makes it 3 lines and the screen cannot delete users by accident. JDK examples: Runnable, Supplier; Kotlin StateFlow exposes read-only to consumers.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Workable { void work(); }
interface Feedable { void eat(); }
class Robot implements Workable { public void work() {} }
interface Workable { fun work() }
interface Feedable { fun eat() }
class Robot : Workable { override fun work() {} }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One interface per method everywhere.
  • Confusing ISP with SRP.
  • Merging pieces after callers depend on them (harder than splitting).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can the old fat interface stay? -> Yes, it can extend the small ones, so splitting is additive.
  2. How does it help tests? -> Mocks only the methods the client uses.
  3. How split? -> By client need, observed from who calls what.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "small interfaces". Senior splits by client usage, notes the additive migration and the read/write split.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 14-method repository blocked refactors because every screen recompiled and every mock was huge.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Dependency Inversion Principle, and is it the same as Dependency Injection?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A classic conflation; the strong answer states the rule, the technique and who owns the interface.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: DIP: high-level policy should not depend on low-level detail; both depend on an abstraction, and the abstraction is owned by the high-level side. Dependency Injection is one technique to supply the implementation. DIP is the design rule, DI is the wiring.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The arrow flips: not OrderService -> MySqlRepo but OrderService -> OrderRepository <- MySqlRepo. If the interface lives in the low-level module, the arrow does not invert, it is just an interface. Swapping MySQL for Postgres then touches one binding, 0 lines of OrderService; with new MySqlRepo() in 30 services it touches 30 files.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface OrderRepository { void save(Order o); Order find(long id); }
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    OrderService(OrderRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }
}
interface OrderRepository { fun save(o: Order); fun find(id: Long): Order? }
class OrderService(private val repo: OrderRepository)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating DIP with DI.
  • An interface for every class "because DIP".
  • Placing the interface in the data module.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you do DIP without a framework? -> Yes, manual constructor wiring in one composition root.
  2. Where does the interface live? -> With the consumer (domain/policy module).
  3. Hexagonal architecture? -> DIP at module scale: ports in the core, adapters outside.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "inject interfaces". Senior says who owns the abstraction, only at boundaries that vary or need a fake.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Domain code importing a JPA entity class made a database swap a six-week project.

questions.promptHtml: How does dependency injection improve testing, and what is the difference between a stub, a fake and a mock?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you test state or over-verify interactions, and know constructor injection.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With constructor injection a class receives collaborators, so a test passes a lightweight version instead of a DB. A stub returns canned data, a fake is a working light implementation like an in-memory map, a mock verifies calls. I prefer fakes for state and mocks sparingly for interactions like "email sent once".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
500 service tests at 80 ms each with a real DB take 40 s; with fakes at 1 ms they take 0.5 s. Constructor injection is preferred because dependencies are explicit and objects can be immutable; setter or field injection leaves half-built objects. Wire everything in one composition root.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class FakeRepo implements OrderRepository {
    Map<Long, Order> m = new HashMap<>();
    public void save(Order o) { m.put(o.id, o); }
    public Order find(long id) { return m.get(id); }
}
OrderService s = new OrderService(new FakeRepo());
class FakeRepo : OrderRepository {
    val m = mutableMapOf<Long, Order>()
    override fun save(o: Order) { m[o.id] = o }
    override fun find(id: Long) = m[id]
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• new inside business classes, then "I will mock it".
  • Injecting the whole container (service locator).
  • 7+ constructor params, which is an SRP smell.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Mock vs fake for a repository? -> Fake; mocks couple tests to call order.
  2. When is a mock right? -> Verifying a side effect such as an email or payment call.
  3. Compile-time vs reflection DI? -> Dagger catches missing bindings at build; Spring at startup.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE mocks everything with Mockito. Senior prefers fakes, keeps tests state-based and wires in one place.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Tests with 30 verify calls broke on every refactor; replacing them with a fake repo cut test churn.

questions.contextHtml:
A nightly job crashes with this stack at 02:14, after processing 4,100 of 9,000 records:

java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
  at java.util.Collections$UnmodifiableCollection.add(Collections.java:1060)
  at com.shop.Exporter.addHeaders(Exporter.java:37)
class Exporter {
    void export(List<String> columns) {
        columns.add(0, "id");        // add header
        // ...
    }
}
// caller 1: exporter.export(new ArrayList<>(cols))
// caller 2: exporter.export(config.columns())   // returns List.copyOf(...)
questions.promptHtml: What is the principle at stake, who is at fault, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in try/catch" or "caller 2 is wrong" with no contract thinking.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which callers pass immutable lists? Does export need to mutate? Did 4,100 records succeed because only some code paths hit it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Copy defensively at the call site that crashes and rerun from the checkpoint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: List in Java does not promise mutability, but export assumed it (an LSP wart in the JDK); a read-only list is not substitutable where mutation is assumed.
  4. How I'd verify: Check each caller's argument type, add a test with List.of.
  5. Root cause: The method's real contract needs a mutable list, but the parameter type does not say so.
  6. Fix: Do not mutate parameters: build a new list inside.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void export(List<String> columns) {
    List<String> all = new ArrayList<>(columns.size() + 1);
    all.add("id"); all.addAll(columns);
}
fun export(columns: List<String>) { val all = listOf("id") + columns }
  1. Prevention: Static analysis rule against mutating parameters; Kotlin List vs MutableList makes intent visible.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not changing the callers to always copy; that spreads the fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did half the records succeed? -> The failing path was only hit for some tenants.
  • Is the JDK wrong? -> It is a known wart: List includes optional operations.
  • Performance of copying? -> Negligible vs IO unless the list is huge.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared constant list wrapped as unmodifiable was mutated by one rare path, crashing a batch at 3 a.m. only on month-end.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swallows the exception.
  • Hire: identifies contract mismatch and avoids mutation.
  • Strong hire: explains optional-operation wart and read-only types.

questions.contextHtml: UserRepository has 14 methods (findById, findByEmail, save, delete, purge, exportAll, ...). The profile screen only reads names, the admin tool deletes, the nightly job exports. Each screen test mocks all 14 methods (about 25 lines of setup). Last month a profile-screen bug deleted a user because someone injected the full repo and called delete by mistake.
questions.promptHtml: How do you split it without a big-bang change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Creates 14 one-method interfaces, or changes all callers in one PR.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which clients call which methods (usage matrix)? Are there external implementers of the interface? Is it a published module?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the screen from calling delete: change its injected type first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Reader, writer and admin/export roles; three client groups.
  4. How I'd verify: IDE "find usages" per method, tabulate the matrix.
  5. Root cause: One interface serves several client roles.
  6. Fix: Add UserReader, UserWriter, UserAdmin; make UserRepository extends UserReader, UserWriter, UserAdmin so existing code compiles. Migrate clients one PR at a time to the narrow type. Finally the implementation class implements the three.
  7. Prevention: New consumers inject the narrowest interface; review check on the constructor type.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No per-method interfaces; split by client need.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface UserReader { User findById(long id); User findByEmail(String e); }
interface UserWriter { void save(User u); }
interface UserAdmin { void delete(long id); void purge(); }
interface UserRepository extends UserReader, UserWriter, UserAdmin {}
interface UserReader { fun findById(id: Long): User?; fun findByEmail(e: String): User? }
interface UserWriter { fun save(u: User) }
interface UserAdmin { fun delete(id: Long); fun purge() }
interface UserRepository : UserReader, UserWriter, UserAdmin

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Partner jar implements UserRepository -> still works, since it is a composite.
  • Read replica for readers? -> UserReader can bind to the replica; split enables it.
  • Is this SRP? -> No: SRP is about the implementer's reasons to change, ISP about client views.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A read-only reporting module injected the full repository and one stray purge call wiped a staging dataset; narrow interfaces made that line uncompilable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: per-method interfaces or one big PR.
  • Hire: role-based split with a composite for compatibility.
  • Strong hire: usage matrix, incremental migration, mentions replicas/safety.

questions.contextHtml:
Module layout in a review:

:domain   (OrderService, Order)
:data     (MySqlOrderRepository, OrderRepository interface, JPA entities)
:domain depends on :data

The author says "we use DIP: OrderService talks to the OrderRepository interface". Yet last week a JPA upgrade forced edits in :domain, and domain unit tests need the JPA jar on the classpath (build 90 s).
questions.promptHtml: Does this follow DIP? What do you ask them to change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, there is an interface, so it is DIP."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do domain classes import javax.persistence? Which module owns the interface? Any other consumers of :data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is a design review. Do not ship more code on this dependency direction.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Interface lives in the low-level module so the arrow does not invert; entities leak JPA into the domain.
  4. How I'd verify: Inspect Gradle dependencies and imports in :domain.
  5. Root cause: Interface owned by the detail, not the policy.
  6. Fix: Move OrderRepository into :domain; make :data depend on :domain; map JPA entities to domain objects at the boundary. Domain tests then run with a FakeOrderRepository in about 1 ms and no JPA.
  7. Prevention: Architecture test (ArchUnit or Gradle dependency rules) failing on :domain -> :data.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Mapping code is boilerplate; acceptable for a long-lived domain, skip for a CRUD admin tool.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mapping cost too high? -> Allow annotated domain objects in a small app; accept the coupling knowingly.
  • Where does wiring live? -> In the app module (composition root) that sees both.
  • Is it still DIP if one implementation? -> Yes if the boundary is real and a fake is needed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A framework major-version upgrade took two sprints because the domain imported the ORM; after moving the interface it was a one-module change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts "has an interface".
  • Hire: moves the interface to the consumer.
  • Strong hire: adds architecture tests and weighs mapping cost.

questions.contextHtml:
class InvoiceMailer {
    void sendMonthly(long userId) {
        User u = new UserDao().find(userId);
        String body = new TemplateEngine().render("invoice", u);
        new SmtpClient("smtp.corp").send(u.email(), body);
    }
}

The team wants a test that checks the email contains the user's name. Currently it requires a live DB and SMTP; a colleague suggests PowerMock to intercept new.
questions.promptHtml: How do you make it testable and what would you assert?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use PowerMock", or test only in staging.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is TemplateEngine pure? Does SMTP need retries? Who else creates InvoiceMailer?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a characterization test in staging only if there is no seam yet; otherwise refactor straight away.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hard-wired collaborators; mixing creation and use.
  4. How I'd verify: Try writing the test; count what must be started.
  5. Root cause: new inside business logic means collaborators cannot be replaced.
  6. Fix: Constructor injection of UserReader, Mail (interface), and keep the pure template as is. Test uses a fake reader and a capturing fake Mail.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class InvoiceMailer {
    private final UserReader users; private final TemplateEngine tpl; private final Mail mail;
    InvoiceMailer(UserReader u, TemplateEngine t, Mail m) { users = u; tpl = t; mail = m; }
    void sendMonthly(long id) { User u = users.find(id); mail.send(u.email(), tpl.render("invoice", u)); }
}
class InvoiceMailer(private val users: UserReader, private val tpl: TemplateEngine, private val mail: Mail) {
    fun sendMonthly(id: Long) { val u = users.find(id); mail.send(u.email, tpl.render("invoice", u)) }
}

Assert on the captured fake: one message to the right address whose body contains the name. Test runs in about 1 ms. 7. Prevention: Rule: no new of collaborators in business classes; wire in the composition root. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No PowerMock; it hides the design problem and breaks on JVM upgrades.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mock Mail with verify? -> Fine here, "sent exactly once" is an interaction.
  • SMTP down at runtime? -> Separate concern: retry decorator on Mail.
  • Too many constructor args later? -> Likely an SRP smell.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A mailer tested only in staging double-sent invoices for weeks; a capturing fake exposed it in the first unit test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: PowerMock or no test.
  • Hire: constructor injection with fakes.
  • Strong hire: explains fake vs verify choice and the composition root.

questions.contextHtml: CheckoutService has a constructor with 9 injected dependencies (CartRepo, PriceCalc, TaxClient, PaymentGateway, InventoryClient, Mailer, AuditLog, Metrics, Clock). Tests need 9 mocks and 40 lines of setup. A teammate proposes switching to field injection with @Autowired "to cut the noise", another proposes a service locator Locator.get(Tax.class).

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks field injection or the locator to hide the number.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does every method use every dependency? Which ones change together? Is the class growing per sprint?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; do not hide the count.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The class has several responsibilities (price, pay, notify); DI is exposing it, not causing it; a tax/price cluster is one concept.
  4. How I'd verify: Build a usage matrix: which method uses which dependencies; cluster them.
  5. Root cause: SRP violation. Seven or more constructor params is a smell, not a DI problem.
  6. Fix: Extract PricingService (cart, price, tax), PaymentFlow (gateway, inventory), PostOrderNotifier (mailer, audit, metrics). CheckoutService then takes 3 collaborators. Clock stays injected for testable time.
  7. Prevention: Review threshold: more than 5 constructor params needs justification.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No service locator (hidden dependencies, global state, hard to undo); no field injection (cannot construct the object without a framework).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Builder for the constructor? -> Hides the smell; no.
  • Aggregate a "facade" of 9 deps? -> A parameter object that groups unrelated deps is the same smell.
  • Metrics and audit everywhere? -> Cross-cutting: decorators or AOP instead of injecting into each class.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 12-parameter service was split into three; test setup fell from 60 lines to 12 and the owners finally stopped colliding in the file.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chooses field injection or locator.
  • Hire: calls it an SRP smell and splits by cluster.
  • Strong hire: usage matrix, cross-cutting via decorators, rejects locator with reasons.

questions.contextHtml: A 300-class Android/backend app calls a global ServiceLocator.get(PaymentGateway::class) inside methods in about 120 places. Tests mutate the global in @Before and sometimes forget to reset, causing order-dependent failures (about 3% flaky, one failure rerun per day). Releases are weekly; there is no freeze. Management wants no big-bang.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate to constructor injection safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite everything to Hilt in one sprint."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which modules change most (migrate first)? Does the platform have an entry point (Application/Main) to act as composition root? Static singletons with state?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the flakiness: reset the locator in a test base class.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hidden dependencies and shared global state cause the flakiness; the migration is mechanical but must be incremental.
  4. How I'd verify: Rank classes by change frequency and by locator call count; run the suite in random order to reproduce flakiness.
  5. Root cause: Dependencies are looked up inside methods instead of declared.
  6. Fix: Step 1, build a composition root creating real objects. Step 2, for each class (hot ones first) add a constructor taking its dependencies and a temporary secondary constructor still pulling from the locator. Step 3, the root passes explicit objects; delete the secondary constructor. Step 4, lint ban on ServiceLocator.get in new code and a counter in CI that must only decrease.
  7. Prevention: The ban plus the decreasing counter.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No big-bang; no migrating dead code.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Framework-created classes (Activities)? -> Use framework injection (Hilt) at that entry point only.
  • Circular dependencies appear? -> They reveal design problems; break with an interface or an event.
  • Is a locator ever OK? -> At the composition root or framework edge only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 120-call locator was reduced by 10 per week with a CI counter; random-order test runs went green before the migration finished.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang rewrite.
  • Hire: incremental, hot classes first.
  • Strong hire: transitional constructors, ratchet counter, root and edge distinction.

questions.contextHtml:
abstract class PaymentMethod {
    /** Charges amount in rupees, amount > 0 */
    abstract Receipt charge(Money amt);
}
class CardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
    Receipt charge(Money amt) { /* ok */ }
}
class WalletPayment extends PaymentMethod {
    Receipt charge(Money amt) {
        if (amt.rupees() > 10_000) throw new LimitExceededException();
        if (balance < amt.rupees()) return null;   // null on insufficient balance
        /* ... */
    }
}

Checkout calls method.charge(total).id() for every method. In production, wallet orders above 10k throw an unexpected exception and low-balance orders produce an NPE; 1.2% of checkouts fail with 500s.
questions.promptHtml: Which LSP rules does WalletPayment break and how do you redesign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add null check and a catch in checkout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does checkout do on failure? Is the limit regulatory? Should insufficient balance be an error or a normal outcome?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Guard in checkout is a stopgap; ship a hotfix to return a failed result instead of null.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Precondition strengthened (limit not in contract), postcondition weakened (null instead of receipt), new exception type.
  4. How I'd verify: Contract test run against every PaymentMethod with amounts 1, 10_000, 10_001 and low balance.
  5. Root cause: The base contract does not describe failure; subtypes invent their own.
  6. Fix: Make failure part of the contract.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
sealed interface ChargeResult permits Paid, Declined {}
record Paid(Receipt r) implements ChargeResult {}
record Declined(String reason) implements ChargeResult {}
interface PaymentMethod { boolean canCharge(Money amt); ChargeResult charge(Money amt); }
sealed interface ChargeResult
data class Paid(val r: Receipt) : ChargeResult
data class Declined(val reason: String) : ChargeResult
interface PaymentMethod { fun canCharge(amt: Money): Boolean; fun charge(amt: Money): ChargeResult }

Checkout asks canCharge or handles Declined; no nulls, no surprise exceptions. 7. Prevention: Shared abstract contract test suite that every implementation must pass. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not catching Exception in checkout; that hides the contract problem.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Limit is per-user config -> still canCharge; it is data, not a type.
  • Why not exceptions? -> Fine if declared in the base contract; declines are normal outcomes, results are clearer.
  • Can a subtype accept more than 10k? -> Yes, weakening preconditions is allowed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A new wallet provider returned null for declines; 1% of checkouts crashed until the failure shape was made a first-class result type.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patches with null check.
  • Hire: names all three broken rules.
  • Strong hire: contract test suite and explicit result type.

questions.contextHtml: Design the notification part of an order system in 10 minutes: when an order is placed, notify by email and push; SMS comes next quarter; push provider times out about 2% of the time and must not block order placement; tests must not send real messages. The interviewer asks you to justify the design in SOLID terms and say where you would NOT apply it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Names five principles without code, or builds an event bus plus plugin loader.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must delivery be guaranteed or best-effort? Can a failed channel block the order? Per-user channel preferences? Message templates?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; it is a design. I set scope: email and push now, best-effort, SMS later.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Variation is in the channel (seam), failure isolation is a requirement.
  4. How I'd verify: Walk through "add SMS" and "push is down": count touched classes.
  5. Design: Notifier interface (D, I) with one send(Message); EmailNotifier, PushNotifier (O); all honour the same contract, failure reported as a result, never a new exception type (L); OrderService only builds the message and receives List<Notifier> by constructor (S, D); the composition root wires them. Failures are isolated per channel.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Notifier { Result send(Message m); }
class OrderService {
    private final List<Notifier> notifiers;
    OrderService(List<Notifier> n) { notifiers = n; }
    void placed(Order o) { Message m = Message.of(o); notifiers.forEach(n -> n.send(m)); }
}
interface Notifier { fun send(m: Message): Result }
class OrderService(private val notifiers: List<Notifier>) {
    fun placed(o: Order) { val m = Message.of(o); notifiers.forEach { it.send(m) } }
}
  1. Fix/extension: SMS is one class and one binding; push timeout is handled by a timeout decorator or async dispatch.
  2. Prevention: Contract test for every Notifier; fake notifier in OrderService tests.
  3. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More files and indirection; no event bus or plugin loader until there is a second producer or external channels; no interface for the message builder.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need guaranteed delivery -> outbox table plus worker, not inline sends.
  • Per-user preferences -> a ChannelSelector chosen by user data; seam unchanged.
  • Only email forever? -> Then delete the interface; a class is fine.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A push provider outage blocked order placement for 40 minutes because notification ran inline; making it a decorated, isolated channel removed the coupling.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lists principles, no design.
  • Hire: working interface design mapped to principles.
  • Strong hire: failure isolation, contract tests, explicit "what I would not build".
